opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it was just a feeling that something was missing. When I started my PhD at Princeton, around 2019, most of NLP was still about benchmarks like classification, question answering, translation. You take an input, you produce an output, and you measure accuracy. That's useful, but it always felt a bit narrow to me. Language isn't just something we use to label things. Humans use language to think, to plan, to act in the world, to coordinate with other people.

Before that I had been interested in reinforcement learning and games, and the dream in RL was always an agent that can do general things. But RL agents were so brittle. You train on one Atari game and the agent can't transfer anything to another. Meanwhile language models were starting to show they had a lot of general knowledge, a kind of prior about the world. So the question that excited me was: what if you combine the two? What if language is the medium the agent uses to reason and decide what to do?

My early work was on text-based games, which very few people cared about. Then came things like WebShop, then ReAct, then Tree of Thoughts. At the time, people would ask, "Why are you working on this? It doesn't beat any leaderboard." And honestly, a lot of the work looked messy. There weren't clean benchmarks, and the models weren't strong enough yet, so results were often weak.

But I think when something is non-consensus, that's actually a good time to work on it, if you have a strong conviction about where things are going. It seemed to me that eventually the most valuable thing about these models wouldn't be answering a question, but doing a task: interacting with a computer, a website, a codebase, the real world. And if that's where the value is, then someone needs to figure out the basic abstractions. How should an agent reason? How should it use tools? How do you evaluate it?

So it was a mix of intuition and taste. I didn't know it would become so hot so fast. I just felt this was the most interesting question, and that if the models kept getting better, this direction would matter a lot.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted agents that could do general things and was excited by combining language models with reinforcement learning to reason and act.

r002.rationale: He describes benchmark-focused NLP, skepticism, and weak results, but does not say that researchers’ division of problems into specialties made general approaches difficult to accept.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a very strategic choice at the beginning. When I started my PhD at Princeton in 2019, the dominant paradigm in NLP was still benchmarks: you take a dataset, you fine-tune a model, you push the number up. And I remember feeling that something was off about that. Language, to me, was never just a mapping from input to output. We use language to do things: to plan, to ask questions, to explore, to recover when we're wrong. None of that shows up when you're predicting a label on a static dataset.

So I started looking at environments where a model has to act over many steps and the world pushes back. Text games were the first thing I touched, things like TextWorld and Jericho. They were a bit of a niche at the time, and people would ask me, somewhat kindly, why I was spending my PhD on Zork. But those games had something I couldn't find elsewhere. You need commonsense knowledge, you need to explore, and the feedback is sparse and delayed. It felt like a toy version of what intelligence actually has to do.

The second thing that drew me in was a kind of frustration with the gap between two communities. The reinforcement learning people had beautiful frameworks for decision-making, but their agents knew nothing about the world. The language people had models full of knowledge, but those models couldn't act. I kept thinking these two sides obviously need each other, and almost nobody was standing in the middle. Being in that gap is uncomfortable, because neither community fully claims you, but it's also where the interesting problems were.

And then GPT-3 came out, and for me that changed the question entirely. Suddenly the prior knowledge was there. The question was no longer "can a model know things," it was "can a model use what it knows to act in the world, and can it reason and act in the same loop?" That's basically where ReAct came from. In hindsight it looks obvious, interleaving thinking and acting, but at the time most people treated reasoning and acting as separate problems.

I'd also say part of it was temperament. I've always been more interested in what a model does than in what it says. If you believe, as I did, that language models would eventually become the thing that reasons and decides, then the environment they're in and the tasks they're given become the real bottleneck. That's a bet on the long term rather than on next year's leaderboard, and I think that's why it was non-consensus. Not because people disagreed, but because it was hard to publish and hard to measure. I just happened to be stubborn enough, and lucky enough with timing, that the field caught up.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting models to use knowledge to act and reason in the world, but does not attribute Yao’s interest to a desire to build general-purpose AI methods.

r002.rationale: It describes a gap between RL and language-model communities and says reasoning and acting were treated separately. It does not clearly explain that the field’s established division into specialties made simple, general approaches difficult to accept.

astra-6.text:
For me, the interesting question was whether language models could do more than produce an answer—could they take actions, observe what happened, and use that feedback to decide what to do next?

That changes the problem quite a bit. If a model doesn’t know something, perhaps it can search for it. If it writes code, it can run the code and inspect the result. Instead of expecting every answer to come from the model’s parameters, you give it a way to interact with the world.

I was drawn to that connection between language and action. Language can help you reason about a task, but acting gives you new evidence and exposes mistakes in your reasoning. Putting those together seemed like a promising direction, even when the models weren’t yet reliable enough to make it look obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says Yao was drawn to combining language and action, but does not attribute that interest to wanting to build general-purpose AI methods.

r002.rationale: The response mentions that the direction was non-consensus and that models were unreliable, but does not explain that researchers’ division of problems into specialties made simple, general approaches difficult to accept.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me in was the gap between generating language and actually doing something. A model could give you a very convincing answer, but could it take an action, observe what happened, and adjust its approach? That seemed like a much richer way to think about intelligence.

Language was particularly interesting because it could connect reasoning with action. You could use it to describe a goal, think through a problem, call a tool, or interpret feedback from the environment. So the question became: could a language model be the core of a system that learns how to solve problems through interaction?

At the time, it wasn’t obvious how far that would go. But that uncertainty was part of the attraction. Instead of only asking whether the model’s next answer was better, we could ask whether it could actually accomplish a task.

r001.rationale: The response describes interest in using language models to solve tasks through interaction, but does not clearly attribute that interest to a desire to build general-purpose AI methods.

r002.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty about the research direction, but does not explain that researchers’ practice of dividing problems into specialties made simple, general approaches difficult to accept.
